project_requirements.title: What the call wants
project_requirements.question: What must the project address, develop and achieve?

cards.title: Central object
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop?
cards.answer:
The project must take an output already achieved by an Interreg North Sea project of 2021-2027 and transform it into a new output for a new target group, field or region.
Interreg North Sea is an EU programme, funded by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF, the EU fund for regional development), for cooperation between regions around the North Sea. An output is a concrete, approved result of one of its projects, such as a tested solution, a pilot, a strategy or an action plan. Call 6, called Take it UP!, funds only small projects that build on such outputs; by the end of the project a new or clearly adapted output must exist. A project may combine outputs from several earlier projects, and the applicant need not have been in the project that produced them.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 4-8 · Special information for call 6
Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

cards.title: Scope
cards.question: Which activities fall within the funding opportunity's scope?
cards.answer:
Taking up and upscaling achieved outputs of 2021-2027 Interreg North Sea projects in at least one of three ways; continuing or extending an existing project is excluded.
Mandatory:
- Build on at least one achieved output of a closed or running Interreg North Sea project of 2021-2027 (the current programme period). Only outputs approved by the programme by the call launch on 1 December 2026 count; outputs from 2014-2020 do not.
- Address at least one of the three capitalisation focuses (ways of transferring the output): a new target group, a new field or domain (for example from one economic sector to another, or from research to the public sector), or a new geography within the programme area.
- Choose one priority and one specific objective of the programme. The four priorities are robust and smart economies, green transitions, climate resilience, pollution and biodiversity, and better governance. A project may apply under a different priority from the original project.
- Address at least two themes: one call-specific thematic focus (increasing competitiveness, strengthening rural areas or building resilience) and one programme spotlight theme (digitalisation, rural-urban linkages, or strengths and challenges of the North Sea basin).
Excluded:
- Simply continuing or extending a closed or running project or partnership.
- Activities already funded by an Interreg North Sea project, and work that duplicates it.
The examples the call gives for strengthening rural areas include rural renewable energy solutions; an energy topic must therefore fit one of these focuses and themes.

cards.title: Problem
cards.question: What type of problem or need must justify the project, and where must it originate?
cards.answer:
A specific, transnational need that an achieved output of an earlier Interreg North Sea project can meet once it is transformed.
The call asks applicants to explain the challenge, why further work on the output is needed, how the need will be met by the end of the project and why transnational cooperation (between partners in several countries) is needed. The need must be specific, transnational and linked to an achieved output, and must not duplicate earlier work. It belongs to the new target group, sector or region the project transfers the output to, for example public authorities, companies or communities in the North Sea region; it must be demand-driven and address common challenges of the region. An application from TenneT's side would therefore have to show that a grid- or energy-related output answers a need shared across North Sea countries.

cards.title: Deliverables
cards.question: Which concrete outputs must the project produce?
cards.answer:
At least one new or clearly transformed output, built on the earlier output and fit for the new target group, field or region.
Examples the call names are testing a strategy or action plan from an earlier project through pilots, or a new action plan based on a successfully tested solution, tailored to a new audience. A minor adjustment of the earlier output is not enough. Projects contribute to the programme's indicators (the measures of outputs and results set out in Fact Sheet 22) and must include communication activities in their single work package. Each partner must disseminate its results as early and widely as possible.

cards.title: Impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
Wider uptake of proven solutions across regions, sectors and stakeholder groups in the North Sea area, contributing to the programme's objectives and to EU priorities for 2024-2029.
Call 6 projects are expected to strengthen the transferability of solutions across the programme area and to contribute directly to the objective of the chosen priority, using the programme's indicators. The thematic focuses link them to EU priorities: competitiveness (innovation by small companies and public bodies, circular economy, digital skills), strong rural areas (for example rural renewable energy solutions and less pollution) and resilience of society, environment and economy to crises. Projects should benefit large parts of the programme area; meeting only the minimum of three countries is a weakness. Approved projects are encouraged to work towards one to three impacts set out in the programme's capitalisation strategy. The call sets no numeric targets.

cards.title: After the project
cards.question: How must the result be replicated, taken up and kept in use after the project?
cards.answer:
The result must be designed for use beyond the partnership, and partners must be ready to support its uptake after the project ends.
- Transfer: the whole point of the call is replication of an earlier output in a new target group, field or region within the programme area, and this must happen during the project.
- Uptake beyond the partners: applicants are encouraged to show how outputs are taken up outside the partnership, for example by involving external stakeholders from the start.
- Durability: small projects must address the long-term effects of the project, and the application form has a section on long-term plans.
- Partner commitment: all partners should be prepared to support activities after the project, especially those that make use of the results.
- Dissemination: every partner must share its results as early and widely as possible, and all results are open access.
The call does not require a business model, standards or a named organisation to operate the result.

cards.title: Number of partners
cards.question: What is the permitted or required consortium size?
cards.answer:
Three to nine partners from at least three countries of the programme area.
At least two partners must take part, or have taken part, in an Interreg North Sea project of 2021-2027, not necessarily the same one. The call encourages more than three countries: a partnership that only meets the minimum is considered a weakness.

cards.title: Partner composition
cards.question: Which types of partners must the consortium include?
cards.answer:
Any legal entity based in the programme area may take part; the call names no mandatory partner types.
The programme area is the whole of Denmark and the Netherlands, the Flemish region of Belgium, north-west Germany, north-west France, south-west Sweden and most of Norway. RVO names governments, knowledge institutions, companies, development agencies and non-profit organisations as examples. Private companies, especially small ones, are welcome but cannot be lead partner. Partners outside the programme area may only join under special conditions. Including partners from the project that produced the output is recommended, and newcomers to the programme are encouraged; partners representing the new field or domain are strongly encouraged. The main users of the results must be involved.

cards.title: Distribution of work
cards.question: How must work and budget be distributed among partners?
cards.answer:
All partners must jointly develop and carry out one work package; each states what it delivers and gains.
Small projects are limited to a single work package. Partners must cooperate in staffing and/or financing the project; acting separately and exchanging results is not enough. Each partner signs a Letter of Intent confirming its financial commitment, and all partners sign a Partnership Agreement that sets out deliverables, shared costs and recovery of wrongly paid funds. The lead partner receives all payments and passes them on. Small organisations may join as sub-partners under a partner in the same country.

cards.title: Coordinator
cards.question: What type of organisation may or must act as lead applicant?
cards.answer:
A non-commercial organisation based in the programme area that works or has worked on an Interreg North Sea project of 2021-2027.
The lead partner (the partner that submits the application, receives all payments and is the contact with the programme) must be based in the programme area and take part, or have taken part, in a 2021-2027 Interreg North Sea project. Private companies cannot be lead partner; Fact Sheet 14 sets out when private organisations acting in a non-profit capacity may. In practice the lead is a public authority, knowledge institution or similar body.
cards.sources: Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 7-8, 11, 13 · Parameters for call 6 small-scale projects; Can private companies get involved?; What is the role of the lead partner?

project_requirements.title: TenneT's position
project_requirements.question: What is TenneT's position within the consortium?

cards.title: Coordinate
cards.question: Can TenneT apply or coordinate, and under which conditions?
cards.answer:
Probably not: private companies cannot be lead partner, and the lead must already be in a 2021-2027 Interreg North Sea project.
TenneT TSO B.V. is a company, even though the Dutch state owns it. The call bars private companies from the lead role and refers to Fact Sheet 14 for private organisations acting in a non-profit capacity; that fact sheet was not read for this report. TenneT would also have to take part, or have taken part, in an Interreg North Sea project of 2021-2027. TenneT could therefore at most lead only if Fact Sheet 14 allows it and it meets the earlier-project condition; otherwise it joins as a partner.
cards.sources: Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 7-8, 11 · Parameters for call 6 small-scale projects; Can private companies get involved?

cards.title: Participate
cards.question: Can TenneT take part without receiving funding?
cards.answer:
The call sets no unfunded role: every partner's costs are reimbursed at the programme rate.
Any legal entity in the programme area, which covers all of the Netherlands, may be a partner. Each partner must state its role and deliverables and sign a Letter of Intent confirming its financial commitment. Stakeholders outside the partnership can be involved in other ways, for example in an advisory capacity; this would let TenneT support a project without joining it.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 9, 12, 16, 18 · Who can apply?; How should partners work together?; Additional points to consider; How to apply
Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

cards.title: Receive funding
cards.question: Can TenneT receive funding, and which funding rate or cost rules apply?
cards.answer:
Yes, as a partner: 60% of eligible costs, calculated as staff costs plus a 40% flat rate.
- Funding rate: all partners in EU Member States are reimbursed 60% of their costs (Norwegian partners 50%), so TenneT must finance the other 40% itself.
- Cost rule: eligible costs are staff costs plus 40% of those staff costs, which covers all other costs; no other cost categories (travel, external services, equipment, works) are claimed separately.
- State aid: partners whose project activities are relevant to state aid (EU rules on government support to companies) must follow Fact Sheet 16; their self-assessment is reviewed at the eligibility check, and the aid scheme may change what a partner can receive. Fact Sheet 16 was not read for this report.
The funding comes from the programme, paid through the lead partner, not from a Dutch national budget; RVO is the Dutch contact point.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 10-11, 14, 23 · Are there special rules for Norway?; Can private companies get involved?; Funding rates and project budgets; Assessment of applications

cards.title: TenneT's likely contribution
cards.question: What contribution would make TenneT credible and useful within the project?
cards.answer:
Our interpretation: TenneT would be most credible as the grid operator that brings an earlier North Sea energy result to a new region or user group.
Useful contributions could be:
- Grid knowledge for transferring an energy output, such as a regional energy-planning method or a rural renewable-energy solution, to a new area where grid capacity and connection limits decide what is feasible, drawing on TenneT's work in the regional Energy boards.
- Data on grid capacity and congestion that makes the new output realistic for the target region.
- Its network with other North Sea grid operators, as in the Offshore TSO Collaboration and the Renewables Grid Initiative, to reach the at least three countries the call requires.
Since the call funds only staff costs plus 40% and at most EUR 1 million per project, TenneT's role would be modest, and it would depend on finding a suitable earlier output and a non-commercial lead partner.

project_requirements.title: Innovation
project_requirements.question: What type of innovation must the project develop?

cards.title: Innovation threshold
cards.question: Must the project produce genuinely new knowledge or technology, or may it integrate and apply existing solutions?
cards.answer:
The project may apply existing solutions, but must transform them into a genuinely new or clearly adapted output.
The programme counts as innovative both completely new approaches and bringing existing technologies and methods to areas or organisations that have not used them. For this call, a minor adjustment or extension of an earlier output is not enough: the output at the end must be new and fit for its new purpose.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · p. 16 · Additional points to consider
Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

cards.title: Innovation object
cards.question: In what must the project innovate?
cards.answer:
Any combination: the call names pilots, strategies, action plans, methods and governance arrangements.
The innovation lies in adapting an earlier output to a new target group, sector or region. The call's examples include methods (a technique for collecting plastic waste), strategies and action plans, and governance: a pilot under priorities 1 to 3 may lead to a project that closes a governance gap under priority 4, and the other way round.
cards.sources:
Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

cards.title: Development stages
cards.question: Which development stages must the project cover?
cards.answer:
Transfer and application of results already achieved: pilot testing, adaptation and uptake rather than research.
The call starts from achieved outputs and asks for their take-up and upscaling; its examples are pilot testing of an earlier strategy or a new action plan based on a tested solution. Research or development from scratch is not the purpose of the call.
cards.sources:
Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · p. 4 · Special information for call 6

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer:
The starting point must be an output already achieved and approved by the programme; the call sets no TRL (technology readiness level).
Only outputs listed as achieved in the programme's reporting system and approved by 1 December 2026 qualify. At the end, the project must deliver a new output that is fit for purpose for the new target group, field or region.
cards.sources: Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

project_requirements.title: Work
project_requirements.question: Which activities or work structure must the project cover?

cards.title: Demonstration
cards.question: Where and under which conditions must the solution be demonstrated?
cards.answer:
The call does not require a demonstration, but pilots in the new target region or sector are one of its examples.
A project may test an earlier strategy or action plan through pilots, or adapt a method to a new geography such as inland waterways instead of coastal zones, always within the programme area. The new geography may be rural instead of urban, inland instead of coastal, islands or remote areas.
cards.sources: Apply in Call 6 (Interreg North Sea website) · Q&A on Call 6

cards.title: Integration
cards.question: How must the activities fit together and with existing systems?
cards.answer:
Everything must fit in one work package with one coherent objective, built on the earlier output.
Small projects are limited to one work package, so all target groups must contribute to one objective. The application must explain how outputs from different projects complement each other and are combined into a new output. Projects must show awareness of related programmes and national and regional actions, explain how they fit into this wider picture and embed themselves in regional strategies. Project funds may only cover work additional to the partners' normal activities.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.question: What must the demonstration prove?
cards.answer:
The project must show that the earlier output has been transformed and that the new need has been met, measured with the programme's indicators.
Small projects use the same indicators as regular projects (Fact Sheet 22). The Monitoring Committee wants to see how the project will test whether the desired change has been delivered, and the final report must describe the contribution to the thematic focuses. Applicants must set realistic targets.

cards.title: User participation
cards.question: How must users take part in the project?
cards.answer:
Yes: the main users of the results must be involved, and external stakeholders should take part from the start.
The call states that a project must demonstrate the involvement and support of the main users of its results, and encourages projects to engage stakeholders outside the partnership from the start, for example to give input on concepts or in an advisory role. Partners representing the new field or domain are strongly encouraged.

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
Up to EUR 1 million per project, with up to EUR 10.6 million from the EU and EUR 300,000 from Norway for the whole call.
- Total project size: up to EUR 1 million total budget, including ERDF and Norwegian funding; there is no formal minimum, and value for money is assessed. Eligible project costs are staff costs plus 40% of staff costs.
- Grant request: 60% of each EU partner's eligible costs (50% for Norwegian partners), so at most about EUR 600,000 per project if all partners are in the EU.
- Funding form: reimbursement of actual staff costs plus a 40% flat rate for all other costs; no lump sums.
The final amount for the call and per priority will be published before the call opens on 1 December 2026.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 7-8, 14 · Parameters for call 6 small-scale projects; Funding rates and project budgets
Fact_sheet_27 _Small_scale_projects.pdf · p. 2 · Budget

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
Partners in EU Member States, including the Netherlands, receive 60% of eligible costs and must fund the other 40% themselves.
- Norwegian partners: 50%, from a separate and limited Norwegian budget.
- Co-financing conditions: each partner covers its own share; the call does not say whether in cash or in kind, but costs are staff costs plus the flat rate.
- Evidence required: a signed Letter of Intent from each partner, confirming its financial commitment, submitted with the application; national authorities also carry out a capacity check of every partner.
cards.sources: Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 10, 14, 18, 23 · Are there special rules for Norway?; Funding rates and project budgets; How to apply; Assessment of applications

cards.title: Budget constraints
cards.answer:
Only staff costs are claimed; a 40% flat rate on top covers everything else.
- Eligible costs: staff costs, following Fact Sheet 2 on staff costs.
- Excluded costs: preparation costs (only staff costs for implementing the project after approval count), and costs of activities already funded in other Interreg North Sea projects.
- Caps: total budget up to EUR 1 million.
- Subcontracting or equipment: the fact sheets on office and administration, travel, external expertise and services, equipment, and infrastructure and works do not apply; these costs are covered by the 40% flat rate. Contracts with consultants for project management must still be awarded through public procurement.

cards.title: Cash flow and financial exposure
cards.answer:
Partners pre-finance their costs, which are reimbursed after reporting, and each must appoint and usually procure a controller.
- Payment model: payment in arrears after two reports, one at mid-term and one after the project closes, each with a financial statement checked by the partner's controller; the lead partner receives payments and passes them on.
- Financial reporting or audit: every partner must appoint a controller (an auditor who checks its expenditure) by the first progress report, usually through public procurement and with its own budget; no payment is made until all controllers are appointed. Funds may have to be repaid if a partner leaves without delivering.

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
One stage: a single application through the programme's Online Monitoring System, submitted by the lead partner.
- Stage 1 — Full application: from 1 December 2026, 12:00 to 15 March 2027, 12:00 CET, submitted by the lead partner for the whole partnership, with a signed Letter of Intent from each partner and an optional visual annex of up to 10 pages.
- Additional procedure: consultations with the Joint Secretariat (the programme's staff) and National Contact Points are strongly recommended but not required; content questions to the Joint Secretariat until 19 February 2027, after that only technical questions. The Dutch contact point is RVO (interreg@rvo.nl).

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
Projects run 18 to 24 months, starting on approval in May or June 2027 and ending by 30 June 2029.
- Maximum duration: 24 months (minimum 18); projects cannot be extended.
- Required start: costs are eligible from the date of approval by the Monitoring Committee, expected in May or June 2027; there is no need to wait for the signed contract.
- Completion deadline: 30 June 2029 at the latest.

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
The Monitoring Committee is expected to decide in May or June 2027.
- Funding decision: May or June 2027, by the Monitoring Committee (representatives of the participating countries), based mainly on the Joint Secretariat's assessment; its decision is final, and a complaint is only possible about the procedure.
- Grant agreement: the Joint Secretariat prepares the project contract after approval.
- Conditions before starting: the Monitoring Committee may set conditions before contracting; all partners must sign a Partnership Agreement and appoint a controller by the first progress report.

funding_timing_submission.title: Application
funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Mandatory submission package — pass/fail
cards.answer:
A complete application in the Online Monitoring System with a Letter of Intent from every partner.
- Application form: in the programme's Online Monitoring System; all sections must be complete before it can be submitted. Optional visual annex: jpg or pdf, at most 10 pages, not text-based.
- Budget: staff costs plus 40% flat rate, in a single work package.
- Partner documents: a signed Letter of Intent from each partner confirming its financial commitment, and each partner's state aid self-assessment.
- Registration: an account in the Online Monitoring System.
An eligibility check follows submission; the output used must be on the programme's approved list.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 18, 23 · How to apply; Assessment of applications
Fact_sheet_27 _Small_scale_projects.pdf · p. 2 · Budget

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
The Joint Secretariat assesses quality against the programme's selection criteria, and the Monitoring Committee decides within the available budget.
- Evaluation criteria: set out in Fact Sheet 18, which was not read for this report. The call stresses a clear need, how the project fits call 6 (capitalisation focus, thematic focuses, transformation of the output), the need for transnational cooperation, the role of each partner, outputs and results, and impact beyond the project.
- Other checks: a capacity check of every partner by national authorities, and review of state aid self-assessments.
- Ranking rules: limited funding may affect decisions; if two projects use the same output too similarly, they may be asked to merge.
Any extra criteria will be announced on the programme website before 1 December 2026.
cards.sources:
Guidance note Call 6.pdf · pp. 19-24 · How to prepare a good application; What is the Monitoring Committee really looking for?; Assessment of applications; How is the funding decision made?

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
Extra rules apply to Norwegian partners, partners outside the programme area and partners doing state-aid-relevant work.
- Exception — Norwegian partners: 50% rate from a limited EUR 300,000 Norwegian budget; contact the Norwegian contact point.
- Exception — partners outside the programme area: only under the special conditions of Fact Sheet 17.
- Conditional — state-aid-relevant activities: the partner must operate under a state aid scheme as set out in Fact Sheet 16; this can apply to public and private partners.
- Conditional — private companies: must accept programme rules on state aid, real costs, public procurement, record keeping and sharing results (Fact Sheets 12 and 26).
- Recommended: consult the National Contact Point and Joint Secretariat; include newcomers and partners from more than three countries.
